received FDA Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations for this indication. The application was also granted Priority Review and received the National Priority Voucher, resulting in an accelerated approval ahead of the February 2027 PDUFA date.

This approval is supported by data from the AZUR-1 trial. The study met its primary objective, demonstrating a significant proportion of participants achieved sustained clinical complete responses at 12 months (cCR12), with data continuing to mature.

Investigator-assessed data, a clinically relevant endpoint, showed 68% of evaluable patients (98/144; 95% CI: 60%, 76%) achieved cCR12. In an exploratory analysis, 76% (110/144; 95% CI: 69%, 83%) of evaluable patients had no evidence of cancer one year or more after treatment. This includes 68% (98/144) (95% CI: 60%, 76%) of patients who reached cCR12 without surgery, plus other participants (n=12) who had their complete response confirmed through tissue analysis after surgery (pathological complete response, or pCR). No disease recurrences have been reported among responders to date, after a median follow up of more than two years.

Data on the primary objective, cCR12 assessed by independent central review, continue to mature. 47% (54/116) (95% CI: 37%, 56%) of evaluable patients have achieved cCR12. An additional 38 participants who are still progressing through to 12 month follow up have already achieved a clinical complete response.

GSK plans to present full data from the AZUR-1 interim analysis as a late-breaking abstract at ESMO Congress 2026 in Madrid, Spain on October 25, 2026.

Current standard of treatment for locally advanced rectal cancer includes chemotherapy, radiation and surgery1, but these can have lasting consequences, including bowel, urinary and sexual dysfunction, secondary cancers and infertility.2,3 For patients with MSI-H/dMMR tumors, a biomarker found in around 5-10% of rectal cancers,
monotherapy could help avoid these interventions.4

The AZUR-1 sBLA is being reviewed under Project Orbis, an FDA Oncology Center of Excellence initiative that enables concurrent review by international health authorities. Regulatory reviews are ongoing in participating countries.
is a programmed death receptor-1 (PD-1)-blocking antibody that binds to the PD-1 receptor and blocks its interaction with the PD-1 ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2. In the United States,
is currently approved for endometrial cancer, rectal cancer and dMMR solid tumors, and is currently being studied as monotherapy in colon cancer and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
